title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Mathematics as the study of patterns
text:
Mathematics as the study of patterns

Key terms: patterns, mathematics, creativity, logical thinking, applications

Mathematics is about finding patterns in the world around us and figuring out why those patterns exist. These patterns can be seen in nature, in daily activities, and even in technology. Mathematicians enjoy discovering these patterns because it combines creativity with logical thinking. Understanding patterns helps us explain how things work and can lead to important discoveries that improve our lives.

Mathematics doesn’t just identify patterns—it also explains why they exist. These explanations can be used in many different situations beyond where they were first discovered. For example, understanding star patterns helped develop gravity theory, which led to space exploration. Explaining patterns helps solve real-world problems and advance technology.

Number theory and number sequences

Key terms: number theory, whole numbers, counting numbers, number sequences, patterns

Number theory is the branch of mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers. One of the simplest patterns is the sequence of counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on. Number sequences like odd numbers, even numbers, and triangular numbers are studied because they reveal interesting relationships between numbers.

Triangular numbers sequence

Triangular numbers are a sequence where each number represents dots that can form an equilateral triangle. The sequence is 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, and so on. The nth triangular number is the sum of the first n natural numbers. For example, the 4th triangular number is 1+2+3+4=10.

Square numbers are numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16, which are the result of multiplying a number by itself (e.g., 2×2=4). title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Definition and naming of regular polygons
text:
Definition and naming of regular polygons

Key terms: regular polygon, side, angle, triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon

A regular polygon is a shape with all sides of equal length and all angles equal. The name tells you how many sides it has: a triangle has 3 sides, a quadrilateral has 4 sides, a pentagon has 5 sides, and so on. The word 'regular' means every side and every corner looks the same.

Key terms: side, corner, counting numbers, sequence

When you count the sides of each regular polygon in order, you get the counting numbers 3, 4, 5, 6, … . The number of corners is exactly the same as the number of sides because each corner connects two sides. This is why both counts give the same number sequence.

If you add the first n odd numbers together, the result is always the nth square number. For example, 1 + 3 = 4 (which is 2²), and 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 (which is 3²). This shows a surprising connection between two different number sequences.

Angles are classified by their size in degrees. A right angle measures exactly 90°, forming a perfect corner like the corner of a book. A straight angle is exactly 180°, forming a straight line, and a reflex angle is larger than 180° but smaller than 360°, curving back on itself.

A number is divisible by another if its prime factorization includes all the primes of the second number, with at least the same exponents. For example, 168 (2×2×2×3×7) is divisible by 12 (2×2×3) because 168 contains all the primes of 12. However, 75 (3×5×5) is not divisible by 21 (3×7) because 7 is missing in 75's factorization.

For a number A to be divisible by number B, the prime factorization of B must be fully contained within the prime factorization of A. This means every prime in B must appear in A with an exponent greater than or equal to its exponent in B. For example, 42 (2×3×7) is not divisible by 12 (2×2×3) because 12 has two 2s, but 42 has only one.

A number is divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4. For example, 8536 is divisible by 4 because 36 is divisible by 4. This rule works because 100 is divisible by 4, so only the last two digits matter. It simplifies checking larger numbers.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding numbers divisible by 4 in a range
text:
Finding numbers divisible by 4 in a range

Key terms: divisible, last two digits, range, check

To find numbers divisible by 4 in a range, check the last two digits of each number. If they form a number divisible by 4, the whole number is divisible by 4. For example, between 330 and 340, 332, 336, and 340 are divisible by 4. This method saves time compared to long division.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Finding numbers divisible by 4 in a range
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Finding numbers divisible by 4 in a range in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility by 8 using last three digits
text:
Divisibility by 8 using last three digits

Key terms: divisible, last three digits, divisibility rule, multiple

A number is divisible by 8 if the number formed by its last three digits is divisible by 8. For example, 8560 is divisible by 8 because 560 is divisible by 8. This rule works because 1000 is divisible by 8, so only the last three digits matter. It is useful for checking large numbers quickly.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Divisibility by 8 using last three digits
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Divisibility by 8 using last three digits in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding numbers divisible by 8 in a range
text:
Finding numbers divisible by 8 in a range

Key terms: divisible, last three digits, range, check

To find numbers divisible by 8 in a range, check the last three digits of each number. If they form a number divisible by 8, the whole number is divisible by 8. For example, between 120 and 140, 120, 128, and 136 are divisible by 8. This method is faster than long division.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Finding numbers divisible by 8 in a range
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Finding numbers divisible by 8 in a range in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Changing a number to make it divisible by 8
text:
Changing a number to make it divisible by 8

Key terms: divisible, last three digits, adjust, multiple

To change a number so it becomes divisible by 8, focus on the last three digits. Adjust these digits to form a number divisible by 8 while keeping the rest of the digits the same. For example, changing 8560 to 8568 makes it divisible by 8 because 568 is divisible by 8.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility rules for 2, 4, and 8 comparison
text:
Divisibility rules for 2, 4, and 8 comparison

Key terms: divisible, last digits, divisibility rule, multiple

Divisibility rules for 2, 4, and 8 depend on the last 1, 2, or 3 digits, respectively. For 2, check the last digit; for 4, check the last two digits; for 8, check the last three digits. Each rule works because 10, 100, and 1000 are divisible by 2, 4, and 8, respectively. These rules simplify checking large numbers.

metadata.topic: Divisibility rules for 2, 4, and 8 comparison

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Why divisibility rules work
text:
Why divisibility rules work

Key terms: divisible, number system, last digits, pattern

Divisibility rules work because of the properties of our number system. For example, 10 is divisible by 2, so only the last digit matters for divisibility by 2. Similarly, 100 is divisible by 4, so only the last two digits matter. These patterns help simplify checking without long division.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Why divisibility rules work
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Why divisibility rules work in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Future divisibility rules
text:
Future divisibility rules

Key terms: divisible, divisibility rule, long division, future learning

In later classes, you will learn simple methods to test divisibility by 3, 6, 7, and 9. These rules will help you check divisibility without long division, just like the rules for 2, 4, and 8. Learning these rules will make solving problems faster and easier.

metadata.topic: Future divisibility rules
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Future divisibility rules in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility rule for 4
text:
Divisibility rule for 4

Key terms: divisibility, last two digits, remainder, long division

A number is divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4. For example, 124 is divisible by 4 because 24 ÷ 4 = 6 with no remainder. This rule helps check divisibility without performing full long division.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Divisibility rule for 4

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility rule for 8
text:
Divisibility rule for 8

Key terms: divisibility, last three digits, remainder, multiples

A number is divisible by 8 if the number formed by its last three digits is divisible by 8. For instance, 1048 is divisible by 8 because 048 ÷ 8 = 6 with no remainder. This rule simplifies checking larger numbers.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Divisibility rule for 8
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Divisibility rule for 8 in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Leap year rules
text:
Leap year rules

Key terms: leap year, divisible by 4, divisible by 100, divisible by 400

A leap year occurs every 4 years, except for years divisible by 100 but not by 400. For example, 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not. This rule keeps our calendar aligned with Earth's orbit.

metadata.topic: Leap year rules
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Leap year rules in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Palindromic numbers
text:
Palindromic numbers

Key terms: palindromic number, divisible by 4, digits, symmetry

A palindromic number reads the same backward as forward, like 1221. To find palindromic numbers divisible by 4, check both the palindrome and divisibility rules. For example, 1221 is not divisible by 4.

metadata.topic: Palindromic numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Palindromic numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Sum of even numbers and multiples of 4
text:
Sum of even numbers and multiples of 4

Key terms: even numbers, sum, multiple of 4, remainder

The sum of two even numbers is always a multiple of 4. For example, 6 + 8 = 14, which is not a multiple of 4, but 6 + 10 = 16, which is. This statement is sometimes true.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Sum of even numbers and multiples of 4
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to analyze concepts related to Sum of even numbers and multiples of 4 in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Sum of odd numbers and multiples of 4
text:
Sum of odd numbers and multiples of 4

Key terms: odd numbers, sum, multiple of 4, remainder

The sum of two odd numbers is never a multiple of 4. For example, 3 + 5 = 8 (a multiple of 4), but 3 + 7 = 10 (not a multiple of 4). This statement is sometimes true.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Sum of odd numbers and multiples of 4
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to analyze concepts related to Sum of odd numbers and multiples of 4 in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Remainders when dividing by 10, 5, and 2
text:
Remainders when dividing by 10, 5, and 2

Key terms: remainder, last digit, even, odd

The remainder when dividing by 10 is the last digit of the number. For 5, the remainder is 0 or 5 based on the last digit. For 2, the remainder is 0 if even, 1 if odd. For example, 78 ÷ 10 leaves a remainder of 8.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Remainders when dividing by 10, 5, and 2
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Remainders when dividing by 10, 5, and 2 in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Special numbers and their properties
text:
Special numbers and their properties

Key terms: prime number, square number, even, multiple

Numbers can be special based on their properties, like being prime, even, or a square. For example, 9 is a square number, while 43 is a prime number. These properties help classify and understand numbers better.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Special numbers and their properties
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to analyze concepts related to Special numbers and their properties in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Composite numbers and their factors
text:
Composite numbers and their factors

Key terms: composite number, factors, prime number, divisors

A composite number has more than two factors. For example, 12 has factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12. Composite numbers are not prime and can be broken down into smaller factors.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Composite numbers and their factors
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Composite numbers and their factors in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Multiples and factors relationship
text:
Multiples and factors relationship

Key terms: multiple, factor, product, divisible

A multiple of a number is the product of that number and an integer. For example, 15 is a multiple of 5 because 5 × 3 = 15. Factors are numbers that divide evenly into another number.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Multiples and factors relationship
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Multiples and factors relationship in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility by multiple numbers
text:
Divisibility by multiple numbers

Key terms: divisibility, multiple numbers, remainder, factors

A number divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10 must meet all their divisibility rules. For example, 5600 is divisible by all these numbers because it ends with 00 (divisible by 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10).

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Divisibility by multiple numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Divisibility by multiple numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Product of two numbers without zero units digit
text:
Product of two numbers without zero units digit

Key terms: product, factors, units digit, multiplication

To find two numbers whose product is 10000 and neither ends with 0, consider factors like 16 and 625. Both numbers must not have 0 as their last digit.

metadata.topic: Product of two numbers without zero units digit

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility by 10
text:
Divisibility by 10

Key terms: divisible by 10, last digit, remainder, multiples

A number is divisible by 10 if its last digit is 0. For example, 570 is divisible by 10 because it ends with 0. This rule is simple and helps quickly check divisibility.

metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Divisibility by 10 in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Divisibility by 5
text:
Divisibility by 5

Key terms: divisible by 5, last digit, remainder, multiples

A number is divisible by 5 if its last digit is 0 or 5. For example, 125 is divisible by 5 because it ends with 5. This rule is useful for quick checks.

metadata.topic: Divisibility by 5

text:
Divisibility by 2

Key terms: divisible by 2, even number, last digit, remainder

A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6, or 8). For example, 124 is divisible by 2 because it ends with 4. This rule helps identify even numbers.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime puzzle rules
text:
Prime puzzle rules

Key terms: prime factors, common factor, arrangement, puzzle

Prime puzzles often involve arranging numbers based on their prime factors or properties. For example, arranging numbers so that adjacent numbers share a common factor. The rules depend on the puzzle's design.

metadata.topic: Prime puzzle rules

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Understanding factors of a number
text:
Understanding factors of a number

Key terms: factor, divisible, whole number, remainder, factor pairs

A factor of a number is a whole number that divides the number exactly without leaving a remainder. For example, 4 is a factor of 12 because 12 ÷ 4 = 3, which is a whole number. Factors come in pairs; for 12, the pairs are (1,12) and (2,6). Every number has at least two factors: 1 and itself.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Understanding factors of a number
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Understanding factors of a number in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime numbers and their properties
text:
Prime numbers and their properties

Key terms: prime number, factors, even, building blocks, prime factorisation

Prime numbers are numbers greater than 1 that have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves. Examples include 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11. The number 2 is the only even prime number. Prime numbers are the building blocks of all numbers because every number can be broken down into prime factors.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Prime numbers and their properties
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Prime numbers and their properties in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Composite numbers and their properties
text:
Composite numbers and their properties

Key terms: composite number, factors, prime factors, divisible, greater than 1

Composite numbers are numbers greater than 1 that have more than two factors. This means they can be divided evenly by numbers other than 1 and themselves. For example, 4, 6, 8, and 9 are composite because they have factors like 2, 3, or 4. Composite numbers can be broken down into prime factors.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Composite numbers and their properties
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Composite numbers and their properties in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime factorisation of a number
text:
Prime factorisation of a number

Key terms: prime factorisation, product, prime numbers, Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, unique

Prime factorisation is the process of breaking down a number into a product of prime numbers. For example, the prime factorisation of 84 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. Every number greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, except for the order of the factors. This is called the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Prime factorisation of a number
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Prime factorisation of a number in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Co-prime numbers and their identification
text:
Co-prime numbers and their identification

Key terms: co-prime, common factor, prime factorisation, overlap, share

Two numbers are co-prime if their only common factor is 1. For example, 8 and 15 are co-prime because their factors are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 5, 15, respectively, with no overlap except 1. To check if two numbers are co-prime, find their prime factorisations and see if they share any prime factors.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Co-prime numbers and their identification
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Co-prime numbers and their identification in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime puzzle rules and solving strategy
text:
Prime puzzle rules and solving strategy

Key terms: prime puzzle, grid, product, prime factorisation, arrange

In a prime puzzle, you fill a grid with prime numbers so that the product of each row matches the number to the right of the row, and the product of each column matches the number below the column. Start by finding the prime factorisation of the row and column products, then arrange the primes in the grid to satisfy both conditions.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Prime puzzle rules and solving strategy
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Prime puzzle rules and solving strategy in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Relationship between factors and prime factorisation
text:
Relationship between factors and prime factorisation

Key terms: factor, prime factorisation, included, divides exactly, primes

A number is a factor of another number if its prime factorisation is completely included in the prime factorisation of the larger number. For example, 6 (2 × 3) is a factor of 24 (2 × 2 × 2 × 3) because all the primes in 6 are present in 24. This helps in determining whether one number divides another exactly.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Relationship between factors and prime factorisation
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Relationship between factors and prime factorisation in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Unique prime factorisation theorem
text:
Unique prime factorisation theorem

Key terms: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, unique prime factorisation, integer, order of factors, break down

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic states that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, except for the order of the factors. This means no matter how you break down a number into primes, you will always end up with the same primes, just possibly in a different order.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Unique prime factorisation theorem
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Unique prime factorisation theorem in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Identifying prime and composite numbers
text:
Identifying prime and composite numbers

Key terms: prime, composite, factors, exactly two, more than two

To determine if a number is prime or composite, check its factors. If it has exactly two factors (1 and itself), it is prime. If it has more than two factors, it is composite. For example, 13 is prime (factors: 1, 13), while 15 is composite (factors: 1, 3, 5, 15).

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Identifying prime and composite numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Identifying prime and composite numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Using prime factorisation to solve puzzles
text:
Using prime factorisation to solve puzzles

Key terms: prime factorisation, puzzle, row product, column product, arrange primes

Prime factorisation can be used to solve puzzles like the prime puzzle by breaking down the row and column products into primes. This helps in arranging the primes in the grid to satisfy the given conditions. For example, if a row product is 30, its prime factorisation is 2 × 3 × 5, which can guide the placement of primes in that row.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Using prime factorisation to solve puzzles
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Using prime factorisation to solve puzzles in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding all factors of a number
text:
Finding all factors of a number

Key terms: factors, pairs, multiply, divisibility, simplify fractions

To find all factors of a number, start by listing pairs of numbers that multiply to give the number. For example, for 12, the pairs are (1,12), (2,6), and (3,4). This method ensures you don’t miss any factors. Factors are useful for simplifying fractions and solving problems involving divisibility.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Finding all factors of a number
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Finding all factors of a number in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Even and odd prime numbers
text:
Even and odd prime numbers

Key terms: prime number, even, odd, divisible by 2, unique

Most prime numbers are odd, but 2 is the only even prime number. This is because all other even numbers are divisible by 2 and hence have more than two factors. For example, 4 is divisible by 1, 2, and 4, so it is composite. The number 2 is unique as it is the smallest and only even prime.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Even and odd prime numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Even and odd prime numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime factorisation of small numbers
text:
Prime factorisation of small numbers

Key terms: prime factorisation, small numbers, break down, prime factors, practice

Small numbers like 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 can be broken down into their prime factors easily. For example, 4 = 2 × 2, 6 = 2 × 3, and 5 is already a prime number. Practicing with small numbers helps in understanding the concept of prime factorisation better.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Prime factorisation of small numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Prime factorisation of small numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Using prime factorisation to check divisibility
text:
Using prime factorisation to check divisibility

Key terms: prime factorisation, divisibility, factor, exactly, primes

Prime factorisation can be used to check if one number divides another exactly. If the prime factors of the smaller number are all present in the prime factorisation of the larger number, then the smaller number is a factor of the larger one. For example, 8 (2 × 2 × 2) divides 24 (2 × 2 × 2 × 3) because all the primes in 8 are in 24.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Using prime factorisation to check divisibility
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Using prime factorisation to check divisibility in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime numbers in real-life puzzles
text:
Prime numbers in real-life puzzles

Key terms: prime numbers, puzzles, games, logical thinking, problem-solving

Prime numbers are often used in puzzles and games to create challenges that require logical thinking. For example, in the prime puzzle, you use prime numbers to fill a grid so that the products of rows and columns match given numbers. This helps in developing problem-solving skills and understanding the importance of primes.

metadata.topic: Prime numbers in real-life puzzles
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to analyze concepts related to Prime numbers in real-life puzzles in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Multiples of a number
text:
Multiples of a number

Key terms: multiple, integer, product, factor

A multiple of a number is the product of that number and an integer. For example, multiples of 3 include 3, 6, 9, 12, etc. Multiples can be found by repeatedly adding the number to itself or by multiplying it with 1, 2, 3, and so on.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Multiples of a number
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Multiples of a number in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Common multiples of two numbers
text:
Common multiples of two numbers

Key terms: common multiple, overlap, multiple, factor

Common multiples are numbers that are multiples of two or more given numbers. For instance, common multiples of 3 and 4 include 12, 24, 36, etc. These numbers can be found by listing multiples of each number and identifying overlaps.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Common multiples of two numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Common multiples of two numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding common multiples using a number line
text:
Finding common multiples using a number line

Key terms: number line, multiple, common multiple, visualization

A number line can help visualize common multiples by marking multiples of each number. For example, to find common multiples of 3 and 4, mark multiples of 3 and 4 on the number line. The numbers where the marks align are common multiples.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Finding common multiples using a number line
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Finding common multiples using a number line in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Perfect numbers
text:
Perfect numbers

Key terms: perfect number, divisor, proper divisor, sum

A perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors (excluding itself). For example, 6 is a perfect number because its divisors are 1, 2, and 3, and 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Perfect numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to Perfect numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Common factors of numbers
text:
Common factors of numbers

Key terms: common factor, factor, divisor, overlap

Common factors are numbers that divide two or more given numbers without leaving a remainder. For example, common factors of 20 and 28 are 1, 2, and 4. These can be found by listing all factors of each number and identifying overlaps.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Common factors of numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Common factors of numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Multiples of 40 between given numbers
text:
Multiples of 40 between given numbers

Key terms: multiple, range, interval, product

To find multiples of 40 between two numbers, start with the smallest multiple of 40 greater than the lower number and continue adding 40 until you exceed the upper number. For example, multiples of 40 between 310 and 410 are 320, 360, and 400.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Multiples of 40 between given numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Multiples of 40 between given numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Identifying numbers with specific factors and digit sums
text:
Identifying numbers with specific factors and digit sums

Key terms: factor, digit sum, range, divisor

To identify a number with specific factors and a digit sum, check numbers within the given range. For example, a number less than 40 with a factor of 7 and a digit sum of 8 is 35 (since 3 + 5 = 8 and 35 ÷ 7 = 5).

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Identifying numbers with specific factors and digit sums
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to analyze concepts related to Identifying numbers with specific factors and digit sums in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Multiples of a number that are not multiples of another
text:
Multiples of a number that are not multiples of another

Key terms: multiple, exclusion, factor, divisor

To find multiples of a number that are not multiples of another, list multiples of the first number and exclude those that are also multiples of the second. For example, multiples of 25 that are not multiples of 50 include 25, 75, 125, etc.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Multiples of a number that are not multiples of another
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Multiples of a number that are not multiples of another in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding two numbers based on common multiples
text:
Finding two numbers based on common multiples

Key terms: common multiple, least common multiple, pair, condition

To find two numbers based on their common multiples, identify pairs of numbers whose least common multiple (LCM) matches the given condition. For example, if the first 'idli-vada' is said at 50, possible pairs could be 7 and 8 or 8 and 9.

metadata.topic: Finding two numbers based on common multiples
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to analyze concepts related to Finding two numbers based on common multiples in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Jump sizes landing on multiple numbers
text:
Jump sizes landing on multiple numbers

Key terms: jump size, common factor, divisor, multiple

Jump sizes that land on multiple numbers are the common factors of those numbers. For example, jump sizes that land on 28 and 70 are 1, 2, 7, and 14, as these numbers divide both 28 and 70 without a remainder.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Jump sizes landing on multiple numbers
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Jump sizes landing on multiple numbers in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Filling missing numbers in a diagram of common multiples
text:
Filling missing numbers in a diagram of common multiples

Key terms: common multiple, least common multiple, diagram, multiple

To fill missing numbers in a diagram of common multiples, identify the least common multiple (LCM) of the given numbers and list subsequent multiples. For example, if the diagram shows common multiples of 3 and 4, the missing numbers could be 12, 24, 36, etc.

metadata.topic: Filling missing numbers in a diagram of common multiples
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Filling missing numbers in a diagram of common multiples in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Understanding the 'idli-vada' game
text:
Understanding the 'idli-vada' game

Key terms: idli-vada game, common multiple, multiple, pattern

The 'idli-vada' game involves saying 'idli' for one number and 'vada' for another, then saying 'idli-vada' for their common multiples. For example, if the numbers are 3 and 4, 'idli-vada' is said at 12, 24, 36, etc.

metadata.topic: Understanding the 'idli-vada' game
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Understanding the 'idli-vada' game in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding jump sizes for a treasure hunting game
text:
Finding jump sizes for a treasure hunting game

Key terms: jump size, treasure hunting, common factor, divisor

In a treasure hunting game, jump sizes that land on specific numbers are the common factors of those numbers. For example, if treasures are on 28 and 70, jump sizes of 1, 2, 7, or 14 will land on both numbers.

metadata.topic: Finding jump sizes for a treasure hunting game
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Finding jump sizes for a treasure hunting game in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Identifying numbers with specific digit patterns
text:
Identifying numbers with specific digit patterns

Key terms: digit pattern, factor, range, divisor

To identify a number with specific digit patterns, check numbers within the given range. For example, a number less than 100 with factors 3 and 5 and digits differing by 1 is 45 (since 4 + 5 = 9 and 45 ÷ 3 = 15, 45 ÷ 5 = 9).

To list multiples within a range, start with the smallest multiple greater than the lower bound and continue adding the number until you exceed the upper bound. For example, multiples of 4 between 10 and 30 are 12, 16, 20, 24, and 28.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Understanding the relationship between factors and multiples
text:
Understanding the relationship between factors and multiples

Key terms: factor, multiple, divisor, product

Factors and multiples are closely related. A factor of a number divides it evenly, while a multiple of a number is the product of that number and an integer. For example, 4 is a factor of 12, and 12 is a multiple of 4.

text:
Identifying prime and composite numbers between 1 and 100

Key terms: prime number, composite number, factors, greater than 1

Prime numbers are numbers greater than 1 that have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves. Composite numbers have more than two factors. For example, between 21 and 30, the prime numbers are 23 and 29, while the composite numbers are 21, 22, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, and 30.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Understanding even prime numbers
text:
Understanding even prime numbers

Key terms: even number, prime number, factors, divisible by 2

An even number is divisible by 2. The only even prime number is 2 because it has exactly two factors: 1 and 2. All other even numbers have at least three factors (1, 2, and themselves), making them composite.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding differences between successive prime numbers
text:
Finding differences between successive prime numbers

Key terms: successive primes, difference, prime number, subtraction

The difference between two successive prime numbers is the result of subtracting the smaller prime from the larger one. For example, the difference between 3 and 2 is 1, while the difference between 97 and 89 is 8. These differences can vary and are not always the same.

text:
Analyzing prime numbers in decades

Key terms: decade, prime number, distribution, variation

A decade is a group of ten numbers, such as 1-10 or 11-20. The number of primes in each decade varies. For example, the decades 1-10 and 11-20 have the most primes, while 91-100 has the least. This shows that primes are not evenly distributed.

Understanding twin primes

Twin primes are pairs of prime numbers that have a difference of 2. For example, 3 and 5 are twin primes because 5 - 3 = 2. Other examples include 11 and 13, and 17 and 19. Twin primes are relatively rare.

Some statements about primes and composites are true, while others are false. For example, it is true that there is no prime number with a units digit of 4, but false that a product of primes can also be prime. Understanding these distinctions helps clarify the properties of primes and composites.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime numbers and their properties
text:
Prime numbers and their properties

Key terms: prime number, natural number, divisors, even number, factors

A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has exactly two distinct positive divisors: 1 and itself. Prime numbers are the building blocks of all natural numbers because every number can be expressed as a product of primes. The smallest prime number is 2, which is also the only even prime number. Examples of prime numbers include 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Composite numbers and their properties
text:
Composite numbers and their properties

Key terms: composite number, natural number, divisors, even number, factors

A composite number is a natural number greater than 1 that has more than two positive divisors. This means it can be formed by multiplying two smaller natural numbers. All even numbers greater than 2 are composite because they can be divided by 2. Examples of composite numbers include 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12.

metadata.topic: Composite numbers and their properties

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Prime factorization of numbers
text:
Prime factorization of numbers

Key terms: prime factorization, composite number, prime numbers, factors, multiples

Prime factorization is the process of breaking down a number into a product of prime numbers. Every composite number can be expressed as a unique product of primes, which is called its prime factorization. For example, the prime factorization of 12 is 2 × 2 × 3. This concept helps in finding common factors and multiples of numbers.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Distinct prime factors
text:
Distinct prime factors

Key terms: distinct prime factors, prime numbers, divisibility, factors, prime factorization

Distinct prime factors are prime numbers that divide a given number exactly and are different from each other. For example, the number 30 has three distinct prime factors: 2, 3, and 5. title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Co-prime numbers

Co-prime numbers

Key terms: co-prime numbers, greatest common divisor, common factors, prime factors, number theory

Two numbers are called co-prime (or relatively prime) if their greatest common divisor (GCD) is 1. This means they have no common prime factors. For example, 18 and 35 are co-prime because their only common factor is 1. Co-prime numbers are important in number theory and have applications in cryptography.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Common multiples and their relation to co-prime numbers
text:
Common multiples and their relation to co-prime numbers

Key terms: common multiples, least common multiple, LCM, co-prime numbers, product

The least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers is the smallest number that is a multiple of both. If two numbers are co-prime, their LCM is simply their product. For example, the LCM of 3 and 5 (which are co-prime) is 15. If they are not co-prime, the LCM is less than their product.

Even numbers are integers divisible by 2, such as 2, 4, 6, and 8. Odd numbers are integers not divisible by 2, such as 1, 3, 5, and 7. Key terms: units digit, divisible by 2, even number, odd number, ones place

The units digit of a number is the digit in the ones place. A number is divisible by 2 (and hence even) if its units digit is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. For example, the number 59 has a units digit of 9, so it is not divisible by 2. This concept is useful for quickly determining if a number is even or odd.

The product of two or more prime numbers is always a composite number because it has at least three divisors: 1, the primes themselves, and their product. For example, 3 × 5 = 15, which is composite. This concept helps in understanding why prime numbers are fundamental in number theory.

Prime numbers can be identified using patterns and rules. For example, except for 2 and 3, all prime numbers are of the form 6n ± 1. The greatest common divisor (GCD) of two numbers is the largest number that divides both of them without leaving a remainder. For example, the GCD of 18 and 35 is 1 because they are co-prime. The GCD is used in simplifying fractions and solving problems related to divisibility.

A pair of numbers is considered safe if their greatest common divisor (GCD) is 1, meaning they are co-prime. For example, the pair (4, 15) is safe because their GCD is 1. This concept is used in problems where two items must be placed such that they cannot be reached by a common factor.

For most prime numbers, the next consecutive number is composite. For example, after the prime 5 comes 6 (composite), and after 11 comes 12 (composite). The only exception is the pair (2, 3), where both numbers are prime. This pattern helps in understanding the distribution of prime numbers.

Key terms: perimeter, shape, area, square, rectangle, dimensions

Perimeter depends on the shape of the figure, not just its area. For example, a square with an area of 16 square units has a perimeter of 16 units, while a rectangle with the same area but dimensions 2 × 8 has a perimeter of 20 units. This shows how shape affects perimeter.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding the perimeter of a house using its overall dimensions
text:
Finding the perimeter of a house using its overall dimensions

Key terms: perimeter of a house, overall dimensions, length, width, addition, fencing

To find the perimeter of a house, add up the lengths of all four sides. For example, if a house is 35 feet long and 30 feet wide, its perimeter is 35 + 30 + 35 + 30 = 130 feet. This helps plan fencing or outdoor space around the house.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Calculating area of a rectangle using length and width
text:
Calculating area of a rectangle using length and width

Key terms: area, length, width, square units, rectangle

To find the area of a rectangle, multiply its length by its width. The formula is Area = length × width. For example, a rectangle that is 5 meters long and 10 meters wide has an area of 50 square meters. This concept helps us measure the space inside a rectangle.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding missing dimensions when area is known
text:
Finding missing dimensions when area is known

Key terms: area, dimension, length, width, division

If you know the area of a rectangle and one of its dimensions, you can find the missing dimension by dividing the area by the known dimension. For instance, if a garden is 50 meters long and has an area of 1000 square meters, its width is 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 meters.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Adding areas of multiple rectangles
text:
Adding areas of multiple rectangles

Key terms: area, sum, rectangle, square units, combined

When two or more rectangles are combined, their total area is the sum of their individual areas. For example, the combined area of rectangles measuring 5 m × 10 m and 2 m × 7 m is (5×10) + (2×7) = 50 + 14 = 64 square meters.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Finding uncarpeted area after placing a square carpet
text:
Finding uncarpeted area after placing a square carpet

Key terms: area, carpet, square, subtraction, uncarpeted area

To find the area not covered by a carpet, subtract the carpet's area from the total floor area. For example, if a room is 5 m long and 4 m wide (20 sq m total) and a 3 m square carpet covers 9 sq m, the uncarpeted area is 20 - 9 = 11 sq m.

Calculating remaining area after removing flower beds

To find the remaining area after removing sections like flower beds, subtract the area of the removed sections from the total area. For example, if a 15 m × 12 m garden has four 2 m × 1 m flower beds removed, the remaining area is (15×12) - (4×2×1) = 180 - 8 = 172 sq m.

Shapes with the same area can have different perimeters. For example, a 6 m × 3 m rectangle and a 2 m × 9 m rectangle both have an area of 18 sq m, but their perimeters are 18 m and 22 m, respectively. This shows that perimeter is not fixed by area alone.

Dividing a rectangle into two equal-area rectangles

Key terms: rectangle, division, equal area, dimensions, area

A rectangle can be divided into two smaller rectangles of equal area by drawing a line parallel to one of its sides. For example, a 12 × 8 rectangle has an area of 96 sq units. Dividing it into two 48 sq unit rectangles can be done by drawing a line 6 units from the side (creating two 6 × 8 rectangles).

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Effect of folding and cutting a square on area and perimeter
text:
Effect of folding and cutting a square on area and perimeter

Key terms: square, folding, cutting, perimeter, area

Folding a square in half and cutting it along the fold creates two rectangles. The total area remains the same, but the perimeter of the two rectangles combined is 1.5 times the perimeter of the original square. For example, a 4 m square has a perimeter of 16 m; after cutting, the two rectangles each have a perimeter of 10 m, totaling 20 m (1.5 × 16).

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Understanding fractions as equal shares
text:
Understanding fractions as equal shares

Key terms: fraction, equal shares, whole, divide, 1/2

Fractions represent equal parts of a whole. When one whole item, like a roti, is divided equally among people, each person gets a fraction of it. For example, dividing one roti between two children gives each child half a roti, written as 1/2.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Comparing unit fractions with the same numerator
text:
Comparing unit fractions with the same numerator

Key terms: unit fraction, numerator, denominator, compare, greater than

When comparing fractions with the same numerator (like 1/2 and 1/4), the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger. This is because the whole is divided into fewer parts, so each part is bigger. For example, 1/2 is greater than 1/4 because 2 is less than 4.

text:

Key terms: fractional unit, unit fraction, denominator, equal parts, whole

A fractional unit is one part of a whole that has been divided into equal parts. Examples include 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and so on. These are also called unit fractions. The denominator tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Real-life examples of fractions
text:
Real-life examples of fractions

Key terms: real-life fractions, sharing, equal size, division, 3/4

Fractions are used in everyday situations like sharing food or dividing items. For example, if 3 guavas weigh 1 kg and are of equal size, each guava weighs 1/3 kg. Similarly, sharing 3 glasses of juice among 4 friends means each gets 3/4 glass.

Adding fractions with the same denominator

When adding fractions with the same denominator, you add the numerators and keep the denominator the same. For example, if you have 1/2 kg and 1/4 kg of fish, the total weight is (1+1)/4 = 2/4 kg, which simplifies to 1/2 kg.

Ancient Indian terms for fractions

Fractions have been used in India since ancient times. For example, the fraction 3/4 is called 'tri-pada' in the Rig Veda. Many modern Indian languages still use similar words for fractions, showing the continuity of mathematical concepts.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Understanding fractions as parts of a whole
text:
Understanding fractions as parts of a whole

A fraction represents a part of a whole. When we divide something into equal parts, each part is a fraction of the whole. For example, if a chikki (a type of Indian sweet) is divided into 6 equal pieces, each piece is 1/6 of the whole chikki. Fractions can be compared by looking at their size relative to the whole. For instance, 1/2 is larger than 1/4 because dividing something into 2 equal parts gives bigger pieces than dividing it into 4 equal parts. Similarly, 3/4 is larger than 1/2. We can arrange fractions like 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and 1/1 in order from smallest to largest.

A fractional unit is a single part of a whole that has been divided into equal parts. For example, if a whole is divided into 3 equal parts, each part is 1/3 of the whole. Different shapes of pieces can still represent the same fractional unit if they are equal in size.

We can measure lengths using fractional units just like we measure parts of a whole. For example, if a strip of paper is folded into 4 equal parts, each part is 1/4 of the strip's length. Combining these parts helps us describe lengths like 2/4, 3/4, or 4/4 (the whole strip).

When fractions have the same denominator, we can add them by adding their numerators while keeping the denominator the same. For example, 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/2, which is the whole. Similarly, 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. This helps us combine fractional parts to find the total.

Equivalent fractions are different fractions that represent the same value. For example, 2/4 is the same as 1/2 because both represent half of the whole. Even though the numerators and denominators are different, the size of the parts is the same.

A fractional unit is the size of one part when a whole is divided equally. For example, if one roti is shared equally among four children, each child gets the fractional unit 1/4. This concept helps in understanding fractions as parts of a whole.

text:

When a whole item is divided equally among different numbers of people, the fraction each person gets can look different but represent the same amount. For example, dividing 1 roti among 2 children gives each child 1/2, while dividing 2 rotis among 4 children also gives each child 2/4, which is the same amount. A fraction can be written as a division problem where the numerator is divided by the denominator. For example, the fraction 1/4 can be written as the division fact 1 ÷ 4 = 1/4. This shows that dividing 1 whole into 4 equal parts gives each part a size of 1/4.

A fraction can also be shown as the sum of equal parts. For example, 1 whole can be written as 1 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. This shows that adding four 1/4 parts together makes a whole. This helps us understand how fractions add up to form a complete whole.

A fraction can be represented as a multiplication fact where the whole is multiplied by the fraction. For example, 1 whole can be written as 1 = 4 × 1/4. This shows that multiplying the size of one part (1/4) by the number of parts (4) gives back the whole (1).

Equivalent fractions can be identified by looking at visual models where the same whole is divided into different numbers of equal parts. To find an equivalent fraction, you can multiply both the numerator and the denominator of a fraction by the same number. title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Subtracting fractions with like denominators
text:
Subtracting fractions with like denominators

Key terms: subtraction, numerator, denominator, like denominators, difference

When subtracting fractions with the same denominator, subtract the numerators and keep the denominator unchanged. For example, 6/7 - 4/7 = (6-4)/7 = 2/7. This works because you are removing a certain number of equal-sized parts from a whole.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Subtracting fractions with like denominators
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Subtracting fractions with like denominators in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Subtracting fractions with unlike denominators
text:
Subtracting fractions with unlike denominators

Key terms: unlike denominators, equivalent fraction, common denominator, subtraction, difference

To subtract fractions with different denominators, first convert them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. For example, to subtract 2/3 from 3/4, convert 3/4 to 9/12 and 2/3 to 8/12. Then subtract: 9/12 - 8/12 = 1/12. This ensures both fractions represent parts of the same whole.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Subtracting fractions with unlike denominators
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Subtracting fractions with unlike denominators in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Converting fractions to equivalent forms
text:
Converting fractions to equivalent forms

Key terms: equivalent fraction, numerator, denominator, multiply, divide

Equivalent fractions represent the same value but have different numerators and denominators. You can create an equivalent fraction by multiplying or dividing both the numerator and denominator by the same number. For example, 1/3 is equivalent to 2/6 because both numerator and denominator were multiplied by 2.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Converting fractions to equivalent forms
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Converting fractions to equivalent forms in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Using Brahmagupta’s method for fraction operations
text:
Using Brahmagupta’s method for fraction operations

Key terms: Brahmagupta’s method, common denominator, numerator, denominator, simplify

Brahmagupta’s method is a step-by-step process for adding or subtracting fractions. First, ensure both fractions have the same denominator. Then, add or subtract the numerators while keeping the denominator the same. Finally, simplify the result if needed. This method works for both addition and subtraction of fractions.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Using Brahmagupta’s method for fraction operations
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Using Brahmagupta’s method for fraction operations in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Equivalent fractions for common denominator
text:
Equivalent fractions for common denominator

Key terms: equivalent fractions, numerator, denominator, common denominator, fractional unit

To subtract fractions with different denominators, we first convert them into equivalent fractions that share the same denominator. This is done by multiplying both the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the same number. For example, to subtract 3/4 and 2/3, we convert them to 9/12 and 8/12 by multiplying by 3 and 4 respectively.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Equivalent fractions for common denominator
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Equivalent fractions for common denominator in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Subtracting fractions with same denominator
text:
Subtracting fractions with same denominator

Key terms: same denominator, numerator, denominator, fractional unit, subtraction

When fractions have the same denominator, we can subtract them directly by subtracting the numerators and keeping the denominator unchanged. For instance, 9/12 - 8/12 = 1/12. This works because the fractional units are identical, so we only subtract the counted parts.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Subtracting fractions with same denominator
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Subtracting fractions with same denominator in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Simplifying fractions to lowest terms
text:
Simplifying fractions to lowest terms

Key terms: simplify, lowest terms, greatest common divisor, numerator, denominator

After performing operations with fractions, we often need to simplify the result to its lowest terms. This means dividing both the numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor until no further division is possible. For example, 6/8 simplifies to 3/4.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Simplifying fractions to lowest terms
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Simplifying fractions to lowest terms in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Brahmagupta's method for fraction subtraction
text:
Brahmagupta's method for fraction subtraction

Key terms: Brahmagupta's method, equivalent fractions, common denominator, numerator, denominator, simplify

Brahmagupta, an ancient Indian mathematician, outlined a clear three-step method for subtracting fractions: 1) Convert to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, 2) Subtract the numerators while keeping the denominator, and 3) Simplify the result if needed. This systematic approach ensures accurate subtraction of any two fractions.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | History of fractions in ancient India
text:
History of fractions in ancient India

Key terms: bhinna, Bakshali manuscript, Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, fraction notation

In ancient India, fractions were called 'bhinna' (broken) or 'bhaga'/'ansha' (part/piece) in Sanskrit. The modern notation for fractions originated in India around 300 CE, as seen in the Bakshali manuscript. Indian mathematicians like Aryabhata and Brahmagupta contributed to fraction arithmetic.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: History of fractions in ancient India
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to remember concepts related to History of fractions in ancient India in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Global spread of fraction notation
text:
Global spread of fraction notation

Key terms: Al-Hassar, fraction notation, unit fractions, Egyptian fractions, global spread

The line segment separating numerator and denominator in fractions was introduced by Al-Hassar, a Moroccan mathematician in the 12th century. This notation then spread to Europe and worldwide. Earlier cultures like Egyptians and Babylonians used fractions, but primarily only unit fractions (with numerator 1).

metadata.topic: Global spread of fraction notation

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Egyptian fractions
text:
Egyptian fractions

Key terms: Egyptian fractions, unit fractions, sum of fractions, numerator 1, puzzles

Egyptian fractions represent general fractions as sums of unit fractions (fractions with numerator 1). For example, 19/24 can be written as 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/8. This method was used by ancient Egyptians and creates interesting mathematical puzzles.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Egyptian fractions

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Fraction arithmetic in ancient India
text:
Fraction arithmetic in ancient India

Key terms: general fractions, fraction arithmetic, Brahmagupta, addition, subtraction

Ancient Indian mathematicians were the first to introduce general fractions (where numerator isn't necessarily 1) along with rules for arithmetic operations like addition and subtraction. This was a significant advancement in mathematics, documented in texts like those by Brahmagupta.

metadata.topic: Fraction arithmetic in ancient India

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Fraction notation evolution
text:
Fraction notation evolution

Key terms: fraction notation, numerator, denominator, horizontal line, Al-Hassar

The modern fraction notation evolved over centuries. Early Indian texts wrote fractions similarly to today's form (1/2). The horizontal line between numerator and denominator was added later by Al-Hassar in the 12th century, creating the notation we use globally today.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Fraction notation evolution

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Practical application of fraction subtraction
text:
Practical application of fraction subtraction

Key terms: real-life application, distance calculation, fraction subtraction, walking distance, auto travel

Fraction subtraction is used in real-life situations like calculating distances walked versus traveled by vehicle. For example, if a school is 7/10 km away and a student travels 1/2 km by auto, the remaining walking distance is 7/10 - 1/2 = 1/5 km.

metadata.topic: Practical application of fraction subtraction

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Comparing fractions using common denominators
text:
Comparing fractions using common denominators

Key terms: compare fractions, common denominator, equivalent fractions, numerator, greater fraction

To compare fractions, we can convert them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. The fraction with the larger numerator is greater. For example, to compare 10/3 and 13/4, convert to 40/12 and 39/12; 10/3 is greater.

metadata.topic: Comparing fractions using common denominators

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Fraction subtraction in time calculations
text:
Fraction subtraction in time calculations

Key terms: time comparison, fraction subtraction, minutes, faster, time difference

Fraction subtraction helps compare time taken for activities. For instance, if Jeevika takes 10/3 minutes and Namit takes 13/4 minutes to walk around a park, we subtract to find who is faster and by how much: 13/4 - 10/3 = 1/12 minutes.

metadata.topic: Fraction subtraction in time calculations

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Unit fractions vs general fractions
text:
Unit fractions vs general fractions

Key terms: unit fractions, general fractions, numerator 1, versatile, ancient mathematics

Unit fractions have numerator 1 (like 1/2), while general fractions can have any numerator (like 3/4). Ancient Egyptians primarily used unit fractions, while Indians developed methods for general fractions, which are more versatile for calculations.

metadata.topic: Unit fractions vs general fractions

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Mathematical notation contributions from different cultures
text:
Mathematical notation contributions from different cultures

Key terms: mathematical notation, cultural contributions, general fractions, horizontal line, standardized notation

Different cultures contributed to the development of fraction notation. Indians created the concept of general fractions and their notation. Al-Hassar introduced the horizontal line. This collaborative evolution led to the standardized notation used worldwide today.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Simplifying results after fraction operations
text:
Simplifying results after fraction operations

Key terms: simplify, lowest terms, greatest common divisor, numerator, denominator

After adding or subtracting fractions, the result may need simplification to lowest terms. This involves finding the greatest common divisor (GCD) of numerator and denominator and dividing both by it. For example, 8/12 simplifies to 2/3 using GCD 4.

metadata.topic: Simplifying results after fraction operations

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Fraction subtraction in distance problems
text:
Fraction subtraction in distance problems

Key terms: distance problem, fraction subtraction, journey, bus travel, walking distance

Fraction subtraction solves distance problems where parts of a journey are covered by different means. For example, if a journey is 7/10 km and 1/2 km is covered by bus, the remaining distance walked is 7/10 - 1/2 = 1/5 km.

metadata.topic: Fraction subtraction in distance problems

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Egyptian fractions and unit fractions
text:
Egyptian fractions and unit fractions

Key terms: Egyptian fraction, unit fraction, numerator, denominator, sum

An Egyptian fraction is a sum of different unit fractions, where each fraction has 1 as the numerator. Ancient Egyptians expressed general fractions as sums of these unit fractions. For example, 3/4 can be written as 1/2 + 1/4. This method was used in puzzles and mathematical problems.

metadata.topic: Egyptian fractions and unit fractions
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to understand concepts related to Egyptian fractions and unit fractions in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | History of fractions in India
text:
History of fractions in India

Key terms: general fraction, Sulba-sutras, Brahmagupta, arithmetic operations, Vedic times

General fractions, where the numerator is not 1, were first introduced in ancient India. The 'Sulba-sutras' show that Indians knew rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing fractions. Brahmagupta later formalized these rules in a modern form around 628 CE.

metadata.topic: History of fractions in India

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Brahmagupta's rules for adding fractions
text:
Brahmagupta's rules for adding fractions

Key terms: common denominator, numerator, denominator, addition, Brahmagupta

Brahmagupta described a method to add fractions by first making their denominators the same. This is done by multiplying the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the other fraction's denominator. Then, the numerators are added together to get the final sum.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Brahmagupta's rules for adding fractions
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Brahmagupta's rules for adding fractions in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Brahmagupta's rules for subtracting fractions
text:
Brahmagupta's rules for subtracting fractions

Key terms: common denominator, numerator, denominator, subtraction, difference

Brahmagupta also described a method for subtracting fractions. After making the denominators the same, the numerators are subtracted instead of added. This gives the difference between the two fractions.

metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.topic: Brahmagupta's rules for subtracting fractions
metadata.learning_objective: Students will be able to apply concepts related to Brahmagupta's rules for subtracting fractions in Grade 6 Mathematics.

title: NCERT Grade 6 Mathematics | Spread of fractions to Europe
text:
Spread of fractions to Europe

Key terms: fractions, Europe, Arabs, transmission, 17th century

The Indian methods for working with fractions were shared with the Arab world and later transmitted to Europe. By the 17th century, these methods became widely used in Europe and then spread worldwide.
